challenges.argument: Option [1] ("Thank you for reading this report, and please feel free to stop by the woodshop...") is the only other option that functions as a closing addressed to the board, and it is in a register appropriate to a report. But it recalls none of the season's concrete results and never mentions the request, so it fails both halves of the stated goal. Option [2] merely repeats sentence 2's zip-tie detail; option [3] is an unsupported generalization in the voice sentence 14 is being revised away from. Minor quibble with the key: it says "a robot that could not turn left," whereas sentence 6 attributes the fault to "Our first drive base," not the whole robot — a small imprecision, not an error in the option's logic.
challenges.key_flaw: Key paraphrases sentence 6 slightly loosely ('a robot that could not turn left' vs. 'Our first drive base... could not turn left'); the justification's 'November failure' and 'donated equipment' are accurate to sentences 1 and 6.

challenges.argument: Option [0] at least offers a results-oriented rationale (winning the Tri-County Build Challenge) that a board might care about, but it is a promise rather than evidence, and it addresses none of the three named values (participation, learning, careful use of money). Options [1] and [2] rest on fun and excitement — the very register of the original sentence 14 ("obviously the coolest club"). Only [3] ties to "attendance never dropped below nine" (sentence 12), the students "teaching the eighth graders" (sentence 11), and "donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits" (sentence 1).

Option [1] keeps the exigence ("because the board asked") and is candid, but its second clause ("most of what we did is easier to show than to explain") undercuts the report rather than explaining why it matters to the vote. Options [2] and [3] give reasons irrelevant to the board's decision (paper records; college applications). The key is the only option that names the budget vote, matching the original sentence 4's "before it votes on next year's budgets."

Option [3] ("This report describes the Gearhounds' first season, including the robot, the members, and the competition in Dunmore") does preview three parts and two of them (the robot, the members) map onto paragraphs 2 and 3. A partial reader might pick it as the 'preview' option. But it is a descriptive announcement, not an arguable claim the report must prove, and its third item (the competition) replaces the actual third section, next year's needs (sentence 13). Option [0] makes a claim but previews nothing and overreaches ("full funding for many years ahead"). Key [1] is the only option that is both arguable and previews build / learning / needs in paragraph order.

Option [1] ("Because attendance stayed above nine, the club will certainly grow to more than twenty members next year") does use the attendance record (sentence 12: "attendance never dropped below nine members") and points toward the club's future, so a careless reader might see it as linking attendance to funding. However, it draws an unwarranted prediction ("certainly") that the data cannot support, and it does not connect to the funding claim. The key's reading — consistency 'even during exam week' shows commitment — is the more defensible inference.

Option [0] ("limited familiarity with engineering ideas") is unquestionably in a formal register suited to a budget committee, and sentences 5 ("spent September and October learning basics") and 11 ("had never used a power drill before") support the idea that members had little engineering background. A reader focused only on tone could prefer it. But it hedges rather than 'admits' inexperience, and it shifts the subject from building a robot to 'engineering ideas,' losing the parallel with the sentence's inventory ("a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and..."). Options [1] and [2] are either self-deprecating to the point of undermining the team or too colloquial. The key preserves the original meaning in measured language.

Option [1] does link to a place student readers know ("Finch Lane residents still remember the two days of rain last April"), and it is vivid and attention-grabbing. However, it shifts the focus to the flood rather than the marsh, and it strands sentence 2's pronoun ("Forty years ago it was Cutler's Marsh") with no antecedent, since no field is introduced. Option [0] keeps 'a field of cattails and cracked pipe' as the referent for 'it.' The key holds.

Option [1] does address cost to taxpayers ("save the town money on mowing, road salt"), but 'school supplies' is unsupported by anything in the passage and the claim is vague, whereas [0] uses the passage's own figures ("180,000 dollars" in sentence 4, "64,000 dollars" in sentence 6). 180,000/64,000 ≈ 2.8, so 'about as much as three floods' is accurate. The only quibble is that 'the town would not have to pay it again' is slightly overstated, but it does not undermine the item.

Option [0] takes a clear position ("The town should pay to restore Cutler's Marsh") but previews only one benefit ('mainly because... flooding on Finch Lane'), failing the 'three benefits' requirement. [1] names all three in paragraph order (flooding, sentences 5–7; mosquitoes, 8–9; lab, 10). No real competition.

Option [0] touches on why the field cannot currently act as a sponge ("the ditches... are the reason the field is so dry and cracked today"), which is tangentially related to flooding, but it does not apply the sponge comparison to the April flood in sentence 6. Only [2] explicitly links both: "Had the marsh been holding water last April, much of that rain would have soaked into it slowly instead of rushing toward Finch Lane." Key is sound.

Option [3] 'Despite controlling floods and mosquitoes,' names the two earlier benefits, so a careless reader might pick it, but 'Despite' signals concession/contrast, not addition. 'Beyond controlling floods and mosquitoes,' correctly frames the lab as an additional benefit. No genuine case for an alternative.

Option [0] retains every fact from both sentences (location, marsh, developer, unbuilt houses, forty years), arguably more than the key, which drops 'past the last cul-de-sac' and 'cracked drainage pipe.' But [0] is garbled: the relative clause 'that lies behind the Brambleton subdivision' is misplaced after 'houses never built,' and 'and was Cutler's Marsh' dangles awkwardly. The stem asks only to keep location and former-marsh status, which [2] does clearly; [3] is a comma splice and [1] is redundant ('in the past, about forty years ago, was once').
